messages:
Alex M.: quick thing — noticed a batch of GPU jobs stuck Pending in us-west-2 for ~20–30m this morning. Karpenter provisioner created nodes but they were non-GPU types and then evicted; pods never landed. anyone else see this?
Priya R.: saw alerts. looks like the provisioner allowed a broad instance type list and spot fallback picked a cheaper non-gpu family. logs show constraints mismatch.
Mateo G.: brief summary from events: Karpenter launched spot instances (p4d not available), fallback to non-GPU because provisioner allowed multiple instanceFamilies -> kube-scheduler bound pods to node but then eviction kicked in when runtime resource requests (nvidia.com/gpu) failed.
Jing Li: that eviction dance is brutal. We should tighten the provisioner for GPU workloads (explicit instanceTypes or required nodeSelector/labels) and set capacityType ordering: prefer spot but fallback to on-demand only for GPU families.
Samira K.: agreed. proposal: create a dedicated GPU provisioner with explicit instanceTypes (p4d, a10g, g5) + taints so only GPU workloads schedule. keep general provisioner for CPU. also set TTLSecondsUntilExpired lower to reclaim stray nodes.
Alex M.: here's a draft snippet for the GPU provisioner — please review:```yaml
apiVersion: karpenter.sh/v1alpha5
kind: Provisioner
metadata:
  name: gpu-provisioner
spec:
  requirements:
    - key: kubernetes.io/arch
      operator: In
      values: [amd64]
    - key: node.kubernetes.io/instance-type
      operator: In
      values: [p4d.24xlarge,a10g.16xlarge,g5.12xlarge]
  provider:
    subnetSelector:
      karpenter.sh/discovery: us-west-2
    securityGroupSelector:
      karpenter.sh/discovery: us-west-2
  consolidation:
    enabled: false
  ttlSecondsUntilExpired: 300
  labels:
    workload-type: gpu
  taints:
    - key: dedicated
      value: gpu
      effect: NoSchedule
```
Priya R.: couple notes — set `consolidation.enabled: false` during migration, but once stable we want consolidation true. also add `capacityType` policy to prefer spot then on-demand fallback for the same instanceFamily; otherwise AWS will pick unrelated types.
Mateo G.: +1. Also we need to watch regional GPU quotas and AMI availability. Ops has seen p4d quotas fill in eu-west sometimes and then cross-region fallbacks cause latency spikes. we should add a metric to track "provisioner_fallback_reason" and emit to datadog.
Jing Li: for the migration plan: 1) create gpu-provisioner in canary cluster 2) label current GPU DaemonSets/Jobs with `workload-type: gpu` and add toleration for the taint 3) run small batch and validate 4) slowly migrate namespaces 5) enable consolidation after 24h stable.
Samira K.: cost note — spot for GPUs saves 60–80% but on-demand fallback for p4d is costly. we should set budget alert when fallback to on-demand > 10% of GPU node launches in 1h.
k8s-bot: deployment gpu-provisioner applied to cluster:canary at 1769510300
Alex M.: thanks. action items I will take: tighten provisioner in canary, create datadog dashboard for fallback reasons, add budget alert. will post updates after first canary run.
Priya R.: i'll prepare a short runbook for rollback (taint removal + revert provisioner) and add pod disruption budget checks so stateful GPU jobs drain gracefully.
Mateo G.: when you run the canary ping me — I'll watch node events and ENI counts. last time we hit ENI throttling when many nodes spun up in the same AZ.
Jing Li: also ensure kubelet evictions thresholds for GPU nodes are tuned (memory vs ephemeral-storage) so we don't evict GPU pods due to transient disk pressure.
Samira K.: noted — cost & quota watch configured. baseline metrics: pending_gpu_pods, gpu_node_launch_fallback_pct, avg_provision_latency.
Alex M.: cool — starting canary now, will post a short results thread in ~1h. :rocket:
